title: Azuma's Inequality for Bounded Martingale Differences
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A martingale whose differences are bounded by c_i has tail probability at most twice the exponential of minus t squared over twice the sum of c_i squared.
short: Martingales with small steps concentrate.
long: Martingales with small steps concentrate. It is the martingale analogue of Hoeffding's inequality.
proof: Apply Hoeffding's lemma conditionally to each martingale difference and iterate.
consequence: It proves concentration for sequential and randomized algorithms.

title: McDiarmid's Bounded Differences Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A function of independent variables with each coordinate change affecting it by at most c_i concentrates around its expectation with a sub-Gaussian tail.
short: Low sensitivity to any one input yields concentration.
long: Low sensitivity to any one input yields concentration. It applies to combinatorial quantities such as coloring counts and matching sizes.
proof: Form the Doob martingale revealing variables one at a time and apply Azuma's inequality.
consequence: It extends concentration from sums to general functions.

title: Berry-Esseen Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For i.i.d. centred variables with finite third absolute moment, the Kolmogorov distance to the normal limit is bounded by a constant times the standardized third moment divided by the square root of n.
short: It quantifies the speed of the central limit theorem.
long: It quantifies the speed of the central limit theorem. The constant is universal but not needed for most applications.
proof: Use characteristic functions and smoothing inequalities to control the approximation error.
consequence: It turns the CLT from a qualitative into a quantitative result.

title: Lindeberg Central Limit Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A triangular array of independent variables with finite variances converges to a normal law when the Lindeberg condition holds.
short: No single variable may dominate the sum.
long: No single variable may dominate the sum. It generalizes the classical i.i.d. central limit theorem.
proof: Compare characteristic functions with the Gaussian expansion under the Lindeberg condition.
consequence: It handles non-identically distributed summands.

title: Slutsky's Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in probability to a constant c, then X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c.
short: A vanishing random perturbation does not change a weak limit.
long: A vanishing random perturbation does not change a weak limit. Products and ratios have analogous versions when the limit constant is nonzero for division.
proof: Use the continuous mapping theorem and convergence in probability of the pair.
consequence: It is used constantly in asymptotic statistics.

title: Continuous Mapping Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If X_n converges in distribution to X and g is continuous on the support of X, then g(X_n) converges in distribution to g(X).
short: Continuous functions preserve weak convergence.
long: Continuous functions preserve weak convergence. Measurability and continuity at the limit points are the key hypotheses.
proof: Apply the portmanteau theorem to closed sets and their preimages.
consequence: It justifies the delta method and many transformations.

title: Delta Method for Asymptotic Variance
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If the scaled estimation error converges to a normal law and g is differentiable, then the scaled error of g of the estimator converges to a normal law with variance scaled by the derivative squared.
short: A smooth transformation inherits asymptotic normality.
long: A smooth transformation inherits asymptotic normality. The first-order Taylor expansion dominates the error.
proof: Apply the continuous mapping theorem to the linear approximation from Taylor's theorem.
consequence: It provides standard errors for transformed estimates.

title: Cramer's Large Deviation Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The sample mean of i.i.d. random variables satisfies a large deviation principle whose rate function is the Legendre transform of the log moment generating function.
short: Rare deviations decay at an exponential rate given by entropy-like geometry.
long: Rare deviations decay at an exponential rate given by entropy-like geometry. It requires the moment generating function to be finite in a neighbourhood of the optimizing parameter.
proof: The Gartner-Ellis theorem yields the lower and upper large deviation bounds.
consequence: It quantifies probabilities far from the typical value.

title: Sanov's Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples satisfies a large deviation principle with rate equal to Kullback-Leibler divergence from the true distribution.
short: Atypical empirical measures are penalized by relative entropy.
long: Atypical empirical measures are penalized by relative entropy. The method of types makes the result particularly transparent for finite alphabets.
proof: Count typical sequences of each type and apply Stirling's formula.
consequence: It links information theory and large deviations.

title: Jensen's Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a convex function phi, the value at the expectation is at most the expectation of the value.
short: Convexity pushes averages upward.
long: Convexity pushes averages upward. For concave functions the inequality reverses.
proof: Use a supporting line at the mean and take expectations.
consequence: It underlies entropy bounds and many moment inequalities.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality in Expectation Form
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The squared expectation of a product is at most the product of the second moments.
short: Correlation is bounded by one.
long: Correlation is bounded by one. It is equivalent to nonnegativity of the variance of a linear combination.
proof: The quadratic polynomial in t given by E(X-tY)^2 is nonnegative, so its discriminant is at most zero.
consequence: It is the workhorse of probability and statistics.

title: Paley-Zygmund Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a nonnegative random variable and any theta between zero and one, the probability that X exceeds theta times its mean is at least (1-theta)^2 times the squared mean over the second moment.
short: A lower tail bound complements Markov's upper tail.
long: A lower tail bound complements Markov's upper tail. It is useful when a random quantity has small second moment relative to its mean.
proof: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the indicator of the event and the square root of X.
consequence: It gives existence proofs by showing positive probability.

title: Kolmogorov's Maximal Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For partial sums of independent centred variables, the probability that the maximum absolute partial sum reaches t is at most the final variance divided by t squared.
short: A maximum of a martingale is controlled by its final variance.
long: A maximum of a martingale is controlled by its final variance. It strengthens Chebyshev from one time to the whole path.
proof: Apply the optional stopping idea at the first hitting time and use orthogonality of martingale increments.
consequence: It proves strong laws and martingale convergence results.

title: Doob's Martingale Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a nonnegative submartingale, lambda times the probability that its maximum reaches lambda is at most the expectation of the terminal value on that event.
short: The maximum of a submartingale is integrable.
long: The maximum of a submartingale is integrable. The L^p version controls the p-th moment of the maximum by the p-th moment of the terminal value.
proof: Decompose by the first crossing time and use the submartingale property.
consequence: It is essential for convergence proofs and maximal functions.

title: Martingale Convergence Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A martingale bounded in L^2 converges almost surely and in L^2 to a limit.
short: Bounded martingales settle down.
long: Bounded martingales settle down. The L^1 version requires uniform integrability for convergence in mean.
proof: Upcrossing inequalities show almost sure convergence; L^2 boundedness gives convergence in norm.
consequence: It underpins likelihood ratio martingales and conditional expectation limits.

title: Strong Markov Property
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A stochastic process with the Markov property also resets after any almost surely finite stopping time.
short: The future depends on the stopping-time state only.
long: The future depends on the stopping-time state only. It is crucial for hitting-time and excursion analyses.
proof: Approximate the stopping time by countably valued stopping times and apply the ordinary Markov property.
consequence: It underlies Brownian motion and Markov chain hitting computations.

title: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A probability vector is stationary for a transition matrix if multiplying the matrix leaves it unchanged; irreducible positive recurrent chains have a unique one.
short: Stationarity means the distribution does not drift.
long: Stationarity means the distribution does not drift. A finite irreducible chain is always positive recurrent.
proof: Existence follows from Perron-Frobenius; uniqueness from irreducibility.
consequence: It identifies the long-run distribution of a chain.

title: Detailed Balance Condition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A distribution and transition matrix satisfy detailed balance when the flow from i to j equals the flow from j to i for every pair.
short: Reversibility makes stationarity obvious.
long: Reversibility makes stationarity obvious. Detailed balance is sufficient but not necessary for stationarity.
proof: Summing the condition over i shows the j-th entry of pi P equals pi_j.
consequence: It is the design principle behind MCMC algorithms.

title: Convergence of Finite Aperiodic Markov Chains
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chain converges to its unique stationary distribution from any starting state.
short: Mixing removes the memory of the initial state.
long: Mixing removes the memory of the initial state. Aperiodicity rules out periodic oscillation.
proof: Perron-Frobenius gives all other eigenvalues modulus strictly less than one.
consequence: It justifies long-run simulation and MCMC.

title: Mixing and Cover Time of Random Walk on a Complete Graph
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A random walk on the complete graph on n vertices mixes in order log n steps and covers all vertices in order n log n steps.
short: Coupon collecting dominates the cover time.
long: Coupon collecting dominates the cover time. The spectral gap is of order one over n.
proof: The transition matrix has second eigenvalue -1/(n-1), and coupon-collector analysis gives the cover time.
consequence: It is the simplest benchmark for mixing-time calculations.

title: Poisson Limit of Binomial Counts
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Binomial(n,lambda/n) distributions converge to the Poisson distribution with mean lambda as n tends to infinity.
short: Rare independent events with stable mean give Poisson counts.
long: Rare independent events with stable mean give Poisson counts. This is the law of rare events.
proof: Take the limit of the binomial probability generating function.
consequence: It justifies Poisson approximations in queueing and reliability.

title: Thinning a Poisson Process
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Keeping each point of a rate lambda Poisson process independently with probability p yields a rate lambda p Poisson process.
short: Independent thinning preserves the Poisson structure.
long: Independent thinning preserves the Poisson structure. The kept and discarded processes are independent.
proof: Independent increments and Poisson counts in intervals transfer to the thinned counts.
consequence: It models competing risks and filtered arrivals.

title: Memorylessness of the Exponential Distribution
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For an exponential waiting time, conditioning on survival past s leaves the remaining time exponentially distributed with the same rate.
short: The distribution forgets how long it has already waited.
long: The distribution forgets how long it has already waited. It is the unique continuous distribution with this property.
proof: Divide the survival function exp(-lambda(s+t)) by exp(-lambda s).
consequence: It makes the exponential natural for Poisson process interarrival times.

title: Gamma Distribution as a Sum of Exponentials
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The sum of k independent exponential variables with rate lambda has a gamma distribution with shape k and rate lambda.
short: Waiting for the k-th arrival sums k waiting times.
long: Waiting for the k-th arrival sums k waiting times. For integer shape the gamma is also called Erlang.
proof: Convolution or moment generating functions multiply the Laplace transforms.
consequence: It connects Poisson processes and gamma waiting times.

title: Uniform Order Statistics Are Beta Distributed
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The k-th order statistic of n independent uniform variables on the unit interval has a beta distribution with parameters k and n-k+1.
short: The k-th order statistic balances k below and n-k+1 above.
long: The k-th order statistic balances k below and n-k+1 above. Its mean is k over n+1.
proof: Differentiate the binomial probability that at least k samples are at most x.
consequence: It underpins nonparametric quantile inference.
